title: Dr. Richa Singh
text:
Hi, I’m Richa.
I’m an educator and researcher in biotechnology at SIES College of Arts, Science & Commerce in Mumbai. Classrooms and labs have been my happy place for close to a decade now, whether I’m explaining a concept, designing an experiment, or watching a student present their first research finding.
My research grew out of a simple fascination: can tiny living things help us build tiny powerful things? That question led me to my doctoral work in bionanotechnology. I began by coaxing bacteria like Acinetobacter into making silver, gold and selenium nanoparticles, and the work has since grown into antimicrobial and anticancer applications, pulling dyes out of wastewater with agricultural waste, and designing adsorbents that can capture microplastics.
If you ask what I’m proudest of, though, it’s the students: the postgraduate dissertations I’ve guided, the undergraduates I’ve walked through their first projects, and the NPTEL mentees I’ve cheered on, several of whom finished as national toppers. I teach across nanotechnology, immunology, cytogenetics, biostatistics and research methodology, and I genuinely enjoy making these subjects feel less intimidating and more exciting than their names suggest.
I’m always happy to connect, whether you’re a student looking for guidance, a researcher exploring a collaboration, or simply someone curious about the nano world.

title: Dr. Richa Singh
text:
Research
My work runs across three connected threads:



Bacteria-made nanomaterials Using Acinetobacter and other environmental isolates to synthesise silver, gold and selenium nanoparticles, tested against drug-resistant bacteria, biofilms, tuberculosis and cancer cell lines.


Cleaning up water Biosorbents made from agricultural waste that strip textile dyes out of water, and nanomaterials that may capture microplastics.


Science education How online professional courses, MOOCs and blended classrooms change teaching practice and learning outcomes in undergraduate science.

title: Research & Publications
text:
Environmental bacteria — Acinetobacter species in particular — can be induced to reduce metal salts into nanoparticles of controlled size and shape. My doctoral and subsequent work established the conditions under which this happens, identified lignin peroxidase and a purified protein fraction as agents of the reduction, and characterised the silver, gold and selenium particles that result. The appeal is that the synthesis runs in water, at room temperature, without the reducing agents that conventional routes depend on.



Biogenic nanoparticles turn out to be active where conventional antimicrobials are struggling. We have shown silver nanoparticles disrupting Acinetobacter biofilms, acting in synergy with existing antibiotics against nosocomial strains, working against Candida albicans, and — with phytogenic silver and gold particles — against Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Selenium nanoparticles from Acinetobacter sp. SW30 proved cytotoxic to breast cancer cells.



Textile dye in water is both a pollutant and a convenient test substrate. Recent work uses banana and carrot peel waste as a biosorbent for procion magenta and black azabache dyes, and gold nanocatalysts to decolorise dye effluent. A current review thread asks whether nano-adsorbents can be made to capture microplastics.



A parallel strand, with colleagues at SIES, looks at how teachers actually learn — the effect of online professional courses on teaching practice, experiential learning that blends MOOCs with project work and internships, and how public understanding of food-contact materials shifts with education.
